# Publisher/player field test

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Installation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md) ·
[Publisher API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md#node-hls-publisher) · [Release evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

The demo is a runnable publisher and an hls.js player with origin-only,
shadow and authenticated peer-first modes. Uploading starts **off**. Receipts
are downloaded locally. Reporting is disabled by default; v0.2.0
can offer explicitly opted-in numeric reports and authenticated
operator controls. See [operations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/OPERATIONS.md). The publisher's signing
key stays on the server. v0.1.0 release assets retain their original behaviour.

## Run locally

From the [current source candidate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md#run-the-source-demo) or a
current main checkout:

```bash
npm ci
npm run demo
```

Open `http://localhost:8787`. Without a media directory, ffmpeg generates
two live H.264/AAC renditions (240p/350 kbps and 360p/1 Mbps video, each with
64 kbps audio and 2 s segments). Requires ffmpeg with libx264 and Node 22+.
Open several browsers, enable uploading on at least one willing participant,
then compare origin-only, shadow and peer-first on another. The demo starts
its own in-memory Nostr relay on `/relay`; it uses the engine's default STUN
unless `--stun` is supplied. It never asks for microphone or camera permission.

`Use origin only` stops the swarm and restores the original fragment loader
while the player continues. Applying settings also stops the previous swarm
before starting another. Uploading and cellular peer traffic require separate
opt-ins. The engine's upload token bucket permits a burst of up to two seconds
of the selected limit; it is not a strict per-second traffic shaper.
Leaving the page stops its swarm. A page restored from the browser's back/forward
cache uses origin until settings are applied again; physical background/resume
behaviour is still a field gate.

## Publish your own media

```bash
npm run demo -- --media-dir /path/to/hls --manifest master.m3u8
```

Use a directory of media you are authorised to redistribute. The directory
is not exposed as a general file server: only the entry playlist, its supported
variant playlists, their media URIs and init maps are served. Symlinks cannot
leave the media directory. Signing requests must match the publisher's current
playlist context; a viewer cannot ask it to sign an arbitrary file or digest.

The Node-only helper is also exported as `relayswarm/hls-publisher`:

```js
import { createHlsPublisher } from 'relayswarm/hls-publisher';

const publisher = await createHlsPublisher({
  mediaDir: '/path/to/hls',
  manifest: 'master.m3u8',
  // secretKey: yourPublisherKey,  // optional; a fresh key is the default
});
const event = await publisher.commitment({
  path: '/media/low/shared.ts',
  level: 0, sequence: 12, discontinuity: 1,
  rangeStart: 188000, rangeEnd: 282000, // end is exclusive, as in hls.js
});
```

Omit both range fields for whole-segment media. The helper derives a fresh,
60 s commitment from the exact file bytes and its playlist records. It reloads
the catalogue at most once per 200 ms and allows at most eight concurrent
signing operations. It caps playlists at 256 KiB, variants at eight, fragments
at 4,096 per variant and signed segments at 16 MiB. hls.js level order is height
then bitrate within the supported single codec/frame-rate family.

The current publisher supports local full segments/ranges/discontinuities,
fMP4, alternate audio, mixed variants, complete parts and warm delta playlists.
AES-128 ciphertext requires explicit opt-in; keys and init maps stay on HTTP.
Remote/query assets, DRM/SAMPLE-AES, subtitles, I-frame variants and cold delta
reconstruction remain unsupported. See [production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md)
for exact schema 2 contexts and the scope of actual Chrome media tests.

Keys are ephemeral by default and in v0.1.0's CLI. Current source optionally
accepts `--publisher-state /private/path/publisher.json`; preserve this 0600
file in an owner-controlled directory for a stable identity across restarts.
Without it, restarting creates a new authorisation and swarm. Current viewers
poll session identity and rejoin while retaining the persistent browser allowance. The demo
does not establish trust in external publishers.

For live OBS ingest and optional independent RTMPS forwarding, use the
[broadcast launcher](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md), which manages persistent
publisher state automatically. Existing media remains usable without ingest.

## Use separate devices and networks

Remote browsers need an HTTPS address trusted by the devices. Configure an
HTTPS reverse proxy to the loopback server, including WebSocket upgrades, then:

```bash
npm run demo -- --public-url https://trial.example
```

The public URL must be an HTTPS origin with no path or credentials. The demo
uses that explicit origin for session and relay URLs; it does not derive it
from an untrusted Host header. Your proxy must forward `/relay` with
WebSocket upgrade support. Alternatively supply `--tls-key FILE --tls-cert FILE`
and `--host 0.0.0.0` with a certificate trusted by all the devices. A plain HTTP
LAN address is insufficient for browser WebCrypto.

Optional `--relay wss://relay.example` (repeatable, at most eight) chooses external
relays instead of the embedded one. Optional `--stun stun:stun.example:3478`
(repeatable) overrides STUN. The loader also accepts host-provided TURN
credentials in `iceServers`; this demo CLI does not supply a TURN or super-peer
service. An unreachable peer should leave the viewer playing from origin.

The embedded relay is for a controlled trial: at most 64 connections, eight
subscriptions per connection, 24 KiB frames, 80 incoming messages per 10 s per
connection, 512 retained events for up to two minutes, and a 1 MiB outbound
queue limit. The HTTP server allows 32 concurrent media responses and 240
commitment requests per 10 s. These bounds do not turn it into a production
hosting service or a Sybil-resistant relay.

## Collect comparable receipts

1. Keep the source, selected quality, device and playback window the same.
2. Play origin-only for at least two minutes and download a baseline receipt.
3. Reload, choose shadow or peer-first, and keep at least one opted-in seeder
   ahead of the viewer. Use the same playback window and download its receipt.
4. Repeat on a different network, then with quality changes, seeks, a late
   joiner, one seeder leaving, and a brief relay outage.
5. Use origin-only during playback and confirm it continues; download the
   receipt so the previous session's stopped resource counts are retained.

Record your device and network labels before downloading. The labels are
viewer-supplied; they do not prove the network topology. A receipt includes
the browser version, startup time, stalls, seek recovery, fragment contexts,
resource timings and engine metrics. It records no peer addresses or private
signing key, but an ephemeral public key can correlate it with relay activity.
Nothing is submitted automatically.

`totals.peerFirstBytes` measures verified media delivered instead of starting
an origin fragment request. It excludes commitment traffic, signalling and
peer protocol overhead, so it is **not net connection data saved**. Shadow
results measure extra sampled transfers and cannot be labelled origin savings.
The upload allowance counter (`bytes.uploaded`) counts full media payloads
accepted for serving, including any transfer later interrupted. It measures
the engine's quota consumption, not acknowledged bytes or total network data.
Use device/network measurements for actual data cost.
Resource timings count same-origin media requests, including init segments
and cache hits. Native-HLS browsers use origin-only playback and report origin
resource measurements as unavailable rather than zero.

Aggregate counts cover the whole page session. Detail is bounded to the last
256 fragments, 60 snapshots (five-minute window) and 64 mode sessions; older
session totals are retained. Stalls exclude user seeks, whose recovery is
recorded separately. Startup begins at the Start playback action.

## Automated coverage and remaining field gates

```bash
npm run test:publisher
npm run test:playback -- --resultsDir artifacts/playback
```

The playback test drives these same controls in real Chrome, using two VOD
renditions with 2 s shared-file ranges and a timestamp reset after 24 s.
It checks both renditions receive verified peer bytes, forward/backward seeks,
discontinuity delivery, range responses, retained hls.js statistics, receive-only
behaviour, relay reconnect, the kill switch and the downloaded receipt. It
compares playback stalls with an origin-only player. Forced quality switches
and returning to automatic selection are covered; optimal or broadly adaptive
ABR scheduling is not established. Loopback tests grant a fake microphone
permission to unlock interfaces; the demo itself does not.

GitHub CI runs this regression alongside both live harness modes. A manual
workflow dispatch with `soak=true` adds a twelve-viewer peer-first run with
three arrival waves, a 180 s final measurement window and sampled resource
bounds. This remains a short loopback soak, not evidence of hours of operation.
The v0.1.0 [completed soak](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md#release-verification) recorded zero
stalls/fatal errors and 68.7% peer-first fragment loads, with uneven per-viewer
benefits. Its recorded receipt does not establish separate-network performance.
The live peer-first fixture caps forward buffering at 4 s (maximum 6 s), keeps
its tampering seeder ahead in availability, and waits for an observed ban
before adding other peers. Its origin-only baseline uses the same buffer
settings. A playhead lead alone does not guarantee that a live-prefetching
viewer will ask the tampering seeder for bytes.
Presence remains swarm-wide; encrypted signals are subscribed to by recipient.
Clients also check the subscription's filter before verifying and dispatching
relay frames, so a relay cannot widen it into an all-audience signal feed.

| Gate | Evidence required |
|---|---|
| Desktop Chrome and Firefox on real networks | Baseline/swarm receipts, quality switches, seeks and origin fallback |
| Physical Android and iPhone | Playback engine identified, consent respected, background/resume and metered-data behaviour |
| Home broadband vs mobile carrier | Selected candidate types plus paired receipts from separate networks |
| VPN or hard NAT | Playback continues from origin when direct peers cannot connect |
| Longer sessions and audiences | Hours of resource/cost measurements, larger churn waves and reachability results |
| Independent-client protocol interoperability | A second implementation verifying the experimental contract |

These field gates remain outstanding until their actual receipts are recorded.
No new physical-device or internet-network result is claimed by the automated
Chrome tests.

---

Source: [docs/NATIVE-TRANSPORT.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NATIVE-TRANSPORT.md)

# Native transport spike

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Installation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md) ·
[API reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md#native-transfer-primitives) · [Release evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

RelaySwarm now has a second, experimental data path for installed Node
applications. It uses Nostr for rendezvous and one-shot authorisation, then
moves the bytes over a Noise-encrypted HyperDHT stream. It does not configure,
contact or emulate a STUN or TURN server.

This is deliberately a bounded spike. It proves that WebRTC is not a protocol
requirement for native RelaySwarm nodes. It does not prove that arbitrary home
networks are reachable, that data remains available after every seeder leaves,
or that a normal browser can open this transport.

## Protocol flow

Protocol version 3 continues to use experimental ephemeral kinds 24170 and
24171. They are not an accepted NIP and must not be treated as stable wire
assignments.

1. Each process creates an independent ephemeral Nostr key and an independent
   HyperDHT Noise key. Neither is the user's social identity.
2. The seeder publishes a signed presence event containing the swarm id, its
   Noise public key and the SHA-256 digest it can serve.
3. The leecher sends a `dial` signal to that ephemeral Nostr key. The signal is
   signed and NIP-44 encrypted. It binds the leecher's Noise key to one request
   id, digest and byte count.
4. The seeder validates the signal, installs a short-lived, one-use firewall
   authorisation for that exact Noise key, then returns an encrypted `ready`
   signal.
5. HyperDHT locates the seeder and attempts direct UDP traversal. The resulting
   duplex stream is encrypted and mutually authenticated by Noise keys.
6. The leecher requests the already-authorised object. The sender re-checks its
   local bytes before serving them. The receiver enforces the expected byte
   count and computes SHA-256 itself before accepting the result.

The relay never receives the object bytes or plaintext dial details. It still
sees event metadata, swarm tags, ephemeral Nostr public keys, timing and source
IP addresses.

The installed API also handles relays that do not retain ephemeral events:
after subscribing, a receiver publishes native leecher presence with `open:
false` and no held hashes. A seeder coalesces live announcements globally to
at most one per second, sharing one timer with its periodic heartbeat. This
presence exposes the temporary Nostr/native public-key link but creates no
transport grant. The exact encrypted dial remains mandatory. See the
[installed API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md#installed-native-client) for verified HTTP fallback,
which is separate from the original CLI spike's failure behaviour.

## What this replaces

For an installed RelaySwarm process, `hyperdht-v1` can replace the WebRTC data
channel and ICE/STUN signalling. HyperDHT supplies its own DHT routing, UDP hole
punching and Noise transport.

It does not remove infrastructure:

- Nostr relays remain the signed rendezvous and authorisation path.
- HyperDHT needs bootstrap/routing nodes. The default client uses HyperDHT's
  public bootstrap set; tests inject a private local bootstrapper. A deployment
  can operate several independent bootstrappers and pass them with
  `--bootstrap host:port`.
- UDP-blocking and difficult symmetric NATs can still prevent a direct path.
  There is no relay or HTTP fallback in the CLI journey. An integrating
  application must implement its own failure handling and selected origin source.

These bootstrap/routing and relay dependencies remain even without STUN/TURN.

## What this does not replace

Ordinary browser pages cannot open arbitrary UDP sockets or run HyperDHT. The
existing WebRTC path therefore remains necessary for browser-to-browser peer
assist. A packaged desktop application, local companion process, browser
extension with a native host, or suitably privileged installed web app could
bridge the native path, but each has a distribution and trust cost.

This is also not yet a decentralised storage network. The process serves an
in-memory content-addressed object while it is online; it does not persist,
pin, replicate, repair or promise availability. A useful Blossom replacement
would need all of those policies plus quotas, abuse controls, garbage
collection and proof that enough independent nodes retain each object.

## Security boundary

The spike fails closed on the following boundaries:

- relay events must have a valid Nostr signature, the exact swarm tag, bounded
  age and bounded payload sizes;
- non-loopback relay URLs must use `wss://`;
- dial details are pairwise NIP-44 encrypted;
- the native listener rejects Noise keys that do not have an unexpired Nostr
  authorisation, and consumes authorisation on first connection;
- request id, digest and size must match across the encrypted Nostr signal,
  firewall authorisation and transfer request;
- individual frames are capped at 64 KiB and objects at 256 MiB; empty and
  excessive object chunks are rejected; pending authorisations are capped at
  256 and active incoming transfers at 16, with a 30 s transfer deadline;
- the receiver's expected digest is authoritative. Metadata supplied by the
  serving peer cannot change it.

The application still has to obtain that expected digest from a trusted source,
such as a streamer-signed manifest or a trusted HTTPS/Blossom descriptor. A
malicious publisher can legitimately sign a malicious object. Hash checking is
integrity, not truth or moderation.

The current receiver buffers the complete object before returning it. That is
reasonable for the spike and small media segments, not for large durable blobs.
A production implementation needs streaming-to-disk, per-chunk verification,
resource accounting, peer reputation, cancellation and origin fallback.

## Run it

Node 24 is the tested runtime.

```bash
npm ci
npm run test:native
npm run poc:native
npm run poc:native -- --relay wss://your.relay --size 1048576
npm run poc:native -- --bootstrap bootstrap.example:49737
```

The deterministic tests start a loopback Nostr relay and a loopback HyperDHT
bootstrap node. They prove the complete authorisation and transfer path without
using external infrastructure. CI is configured to run them on current GitHub
Windows, Linux and macOS runners. The v0.1.0 native suite passed on all three
platforms ([release-main run 38233694634](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/actions/runs/38233694634)); that proves those tests rather than packaging,
firewall prompts or real home-network reachability.

Still required before choosing this for production:

- real home-to-home tests across varied NATs, VPNs, IPv4/IPv6 and UDP-blocked
  networks;
- suspend/resume, sleep, network change and long-running resource tests;
- executable packaging and firewall-prompt testing on all three operating
  systems;
- protocol interop with a genuinely independent implementation;
- dependency and native-binary supply-chain review;
- a signed content manifest and a durable storage/replication policy.

## Installed client and verified HTTP fallback

The current source additionally supplies `relayswarm-native` and the
`relayswarm/native-client` API. It requires an independently trusted digest,
size, seeder allowlist and explicit endpoint policy. A bounded native attempt
precedes HTTPS fallback; redirects, excess bytes and wrong digests are refused.
Cancellation stops rather than starting fallback. The executable creates a
new verified output atomically and requires installed Node. The original PoC
journey described above retains its original behaviour. See
[production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md#installed-native-client) and
[API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md#installed-native-client).

Source: [docs/THREAT-MODEL.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/THREAT-MODEL.md)

# RelaySwarm threat model

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Release evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) ·
[Integration](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md)

This describes the implemented experimental boundaries and the remaining
adversarial work at v0.2.0. Passing named regression cases does not establish
production security or completion of the threat model. The original CLI,
browser loader and native path have different trust assumptions.

## Implemented boundaries

The browser peer-first loader verifies an author-signed, canonical and
expiring segment commitment, including stream/rendition/sequence/discontinuity/
part and object identity. It checks the experimental publisher redistribution
tag; current source also permits explicitly author-scoped delegated signers.
The original CLI PoC is unchanged.

Regression tests cover request floods, empty/excessive chunks, upload stalls,
expired admission on retries, delayed admission during shutdown, relay startup
recovery, late reconnects, commitment substitution and origin fallback. Real
Chrome tests require tampering detection, compare playback stalls with a
baseline, check shutdown resources and prove peer-first avoids origin requests.
Native nodes bound pending authorisations and active transfers.

The example Node publisher signs only a full-segment context present in its
local playlists, including the exact byte range and discontinuity. It serves
listed media rather than arbitrary directory files and rejects symlink escapes.
Its key stays on the server; current source can persist a private identity
in an owner-controlled 0600 file. This is an example publisher,
not a trusted-stream discovery service: a real host must still establish which
stream author it trusts. The demo's relay and HTTP endpoints have resource bounds. Current source
adds key-possession tickets and live revocation; open issuance does not prove
unique participants or complete Sybil resistance. Receipts
stay in the browser until downloaded; optional reporting requires viewer
opt-in and accepts only bounded numeric summaries, without a swarm public key.
These controls do not establish unique participants or net cost.

These are specific tested boundaries, not completion of the adversarial suite
below. Sybil resistance, broad NAT/mobile coverage and independent-client
protocol interoperability remain outstanding.

## Assets

- **Segment integrity** - a viewer must never play bytes the streamer did
  not produce.
- **Viewer availability** - peer assistance must degrade to plain HLS, not
  to a broken player.
- **Viewer privacy floor** - swarm events must carry no social npub and use
  independent per-session keys, and non-participation (origin-only mode)
  must be free. This is pseudonymity, not anonymity; relays and network
  observers may still correlate swarm activity with a viewer's other Nostr
  use through shared connections, IP addresses and timing, and a client
  that reuses one relay connection for both makes that correlation trivial.
  The browser loader creates its own swarm relay pool, but shared IPs/timing
  still permit correlation; applications using the lower-level session API
  must also consider which connections they share.
- **Origin capacity** - the resource the swarm exists to protect.

## The core defence: authenticated segment commitments

The original PoC verifies a SHA-256 hash supplied by the sending peer. That
proves transport, not provenance: a malicious seeder controls bytes and hash.
Shadow mode instead compares with origin bytes, while the browser peer-first
loader requires a commitment signed by the **same author as the selected
kind-30311 stream event**. It binds stream/event identity, swarm, rendition,
sequence, discontinuity, part, segment key, digest, size and expiry. Wrong
bytes fail verification, the peer is banned, and the normal origin loader is
the fallback. Receiving a digest over HTTPS alone does not satisfy the
current peer-first signature contract.

The verifier requires fixed field order and exact canonical JSON with the
`relayswarm-segment-v1` domain and schema version 1. It rejects altered fields,
other signers, expired/stale events and substituted media contexts. The precise
contract is in [INTEGRATION.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md#authenticated-peer-first-loading).
Current source implements author-scoped expiring commitment keys and a
host-supplied revocation view; [production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md)
describes the trust and availability boundary.
The host still establishes which publisher it trusts. A malicious authorised
publisher can sign harmful bytes; cryptographic integrity is not moderation.

Streams also carry an explicit **peer-redistribution authorised** flag;
absent it, clients do not form a swarm. Peer assistance is something a
publisher opts into for their own stream, not something viewers may switch
on for any HLS URL.

## Adversarial suite

These are areas for the full adversarial suite. Some individual cases are
already regressed above; broader combinations remain outstanding:

- Wrong bytes under every digest arrangement (peer-supplied, stale,
  cross-rendition, cross-stream).
- Replay of expired segments and cross-rendition substitution.
- Sybil presence floods - thousands of fake peers announcing.
- Malformed and oversized SDP payloads.
- Resource exhaustion - connection floods, chunk floods, slow-loris peers.
- Relay withholding and selective event dropping.
- A compromised super-peer serving many viewers.

## Client-side resource defence

Event spam is not only the relays' rate-limiting problem; a client must
defend itself. The engine bounds its subscriptions, enforces event-size
limits, budgets concurrent dials and caps queues. Relay frames must match a
live subscription id/filter before signature validation and dispatch; signals
are subscribed to by recipient, while presence remains swarm-wide. The loader
bounds admission checks and transfers and uses availability, rotation/referrals
and deadlines. This is not an implemented reputation or Sybil-resistance system:
validly signed fake presence can still consume bounded client work.

## Out of scope, stated plainly

- **Metadata privacy.** NIP-44 hides event payloads, not metadata; relays
  see kinds, tags, timing and connecting IPs, and anyone who knows a public
  stream's identifier can observe its swarm activity. See the privacy
  section of the [README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/README.md).
- **WebRTC protocol fingerprinting.** A state that filters DTLS takes the
  swarm down to plain-HLS fallback; resistance is future work, not quietly
  claimed here.
- **A hidden origin.** The swarm distributes egress, not ingest. No dedicated
  onion-service support or origin-concealment feature is implemented.

---

Source: [docs/FAQ.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FAQ.md)

# RelaySwarm FAQ

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Getting started](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md) ·
[Evidence and gaps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

## What is released?

[v0.2.0](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/releases/tag/v0.2.0) is an
experimental GitHub prerelease with an installable tarball, a standalone browser
ESM bundle and checksums. It includes the browser loader, local publisher/player
and native transfer PoC, plus the live broadcaster, private publisher state and
operator controls. The npm registry remains unpublished; the release does
not provision hosting. See
[Getting started](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md) and [the broadcaster guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md).

## Why use Nostr instead of a tracker?

RelaySwarm reuses application-selected Nostr relays for peer discovery and
signalling. It still needs rendezvous infrastructure. P2P Media Loader instead
uses [WebTorrent-compatible trackers](https://github.com/Novage/p2p-media-loader/blob/main/FAQ.md#what-is-tracker),
which may also be redundant or self-hosted. The distinction is the discovery
protocol and its fit with Nostr applications, not the elimination of operators.

## Why not combine Trystero and P2P Media Loader?

Those projects provide useful building blocks. A host would still need to
integrate stream identity, signed segment provenance, origin deadlines,
admission, upload consent and lifecycle handling. RelaySwarm implements a
bounded example of that layer; it does not claim that the alternatives cannot
implement it. [Landscape](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/LANDSCAPE.md) compares their documented roles.

## Does it support MoQ or replace a CDN?

The current paths are WebRTC and native HyperDHT. MoQ integration is unimplemented.
The HTTP origin or CDN still supplies manifests, initial media and fallback;
RelaySwarm can reduce particular origin media loads when suitable peers exist.
It does not remove ingest, origin hosting or operator costs.

## Does NIP-53 automatically configure the swarm?

No. The host selects trusted authors, allowed media origins, the swarm id, relays
and ICE servers. The released loader accepts the selected event. An optional
adapter in v0.2.0 filters a host-supplied query using those explicit
allowlists; it does not choose infrastructure or establish trust in arbitrary
publishers. NIP-53 can carry relay information; the redistribution tag and
commitment kind are RelaySwarm's experimental contract.

## Can it send a broadcast to YouTube?

The v0.2.0 broadcaster can send the same H.264/AAC source to a separately
configured RTMPS endpoint while producing HLS for RelaySwarm viewers. That
forwarder has its own process and retries. A valid platform stream key, account
configuration and an actual platform playback test are still needed. YouTube
does not participate in the viewer peer swarm. See [broadcasting](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md).

## Is signalling encrypted?

The original `poc.mjs` signs **plaintext SDP**. The browser loader and shared
version-3 `RelaySwarmSession` use pairwise NIP-44-encrypted signals. The native
path encrypts its dial authorisation and transfers bytes over Noise.
WebRTC data-channel encryption and SDP encryption are separate properties.
Relays still see event kinds, tags, timing and connecting addresses.

## Can a peer poison a video segment?

The browser peer-first path accepts bytes only after verifying an expiring
commitment signed by the selected stream-event author and matching the exact
stream, rendition, sequence, discontinuity, part, segment key, size and digest.
Invalid bytes are discarded and the peer is banned; failures use the original
HTTP loader. The publisher must authorise redistribution explicitly.

Shadow mode compares peer bytes with origin bytes. The original CLI's
same-peer digest detects corruption but cannot authenticate a malicious
seeder. The native receiver needs a digest from a trusted application source.
Hashes do not establish whether content is truthful or safe.

## Can I upload without the viewer opting in?

Contribution defaults to off. A host must obtain explicit opt-in before setting
`serve: true`; the demo has a separate upload checkbox and limit selector.
Known cellular connections are excluded by default, but connection detection
is advisory and missing in some browsers. Publisher permission and viewer
consent are both required. The upload token bucket permits a burst of up to
two seconds of its configured allowance.

## Does receive-only mean private?

Receive-only disables uploading, but still joins the swarm and can reveal the
viewer's address to connected peers. Ephemeral keys provide pseudonymity,
not anonymity. A public swarm identifier lets observers correlate presence.
`mode: 'off'` or `stop()` provides origin-only playback without swarm sockets,
events or peer connections. The origin still sees ordinary HLS requests.

## Do phones and Safari work?

The earlier spikes recorded desktop Chrome/Safari transfers and limited phone
origin-playback observations. They did not validate the current signed
peer-first loader on iPhone or Android. The new regression uses desktop Chrome
on loopback. The demo uses native origin-only HLS where the browser supports
it but hls.js does not; origin resource measurements then report unavailable.
Physical playback, consent, metered data and background/resume remain
[field gates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md#automated-coverage-and-remaining-field-gates).

## What happens when peers, relays or WebRTC are blocked?

The original HTTP fragment loader remains the fallback. Missing availability,
invalid commitments, corruption and peer deadlines lead to origin. An origin
outage can still stop playback; the swarm is not durable storage. Relays may
change policies, reject kinds or rate-limit. Historical public-relay acceptance
does not guarantee future service. A deployment should choose and test its own
relay and ICE policy.

## Does it use STUN, TURN or super-peers?

The browser loader defaults to Google's public STUN endpoint and accepts host
`iceServers`; the demo accepts `--stun`. Hosts can supply TURN credentials
through `iceServers`; no managed TURN or super-peer service is supplied.
Difficult NATs can fall back to origin. Native HyperDHT uses its own
bootstrap/routing infrastructure rather than STUN/TURN and has no automatic
origin fallback in its CLI journey. See [Native transport](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NATIVE-TRANSPORT.md).

## Can I use HyperDHT in a normal browser?

No. This native implementation requires installed Node applications and UDP
access. Browser pages use WebRTC. Installed companion processes would need
their own integration and distribution work.

## Does RelaySwarmKit interoperate with this release?

That has not been established. The separate
[Swift project's README](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm-kit) describes
version-2 signalling; this repository uses version 3 for the shared session.
Shared event kinds and successful NIP-44 vectors do not prove matching wire
envelopes, native transport or signed HLS commitments. A RelaySwarm protocol draft and tested adapter exist, but no RelaySwarm NIP
is accepted yet.

## Do the receipts measure money or data saved?

`peerFirstBytes` measures verified media delivered in place of starting an
origin fragment load. It excludes commitment, signalling and protocol traffic.
Shadow transfers add traffic. `bytes.uploaded` counts full payloads accepted
against the quota, including interrupted transfers; it is not acknowledged
network delivery. Receipts stay local until downloaded. Use paired device/network
measurements to establish total data cost. See [receipt interpretation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FIELD-TEST.md#collect-comparable-receipts).

## What remains before production?

Physical devices, separate-network/NAT trials, sustained resource and cost
measurements, broader adaptive bitrate and fMP4 coverage, stronger adversarial
testing and independent-client interoperability. [Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) records
which evidence exists. There is no prediction that audience upload capacity
will cover a given deployment.

## What permission does a contributing viewer need?

A contributing viewer redistributes media. The publisher authorisation tag
expresses the publisher's opt-in; it does not establish ownership of every
right or settle a viewer's legal/contractual obligations. The demo should be
used with media participants are authorised to redistribute. Host policy and
explicit viewer consent remain application responsibilities.

## What does the current production candidate add?

[Production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md) covers wider HLS, scoped delegation,
full linked stream advertisements, bounded admission, persistent browser upload
budgets, durable idempotent reports, worker supervision and native HTTP fallback.
[Delivery requirements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md) separates implementation from
publication, physical devices, varied networks and sustained acceptance.

---

Source: [docs/LANDSCAPE.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/LANDSCAPE.md)

# RelaySwarm landscape

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [FAQ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/FAQ.md) · [Current scope](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

Documentation comparison refreshed on 12 October 2026 from the linked primary
sources. This is a comparison of documented roles, not a performance benchmark,
an exhaustive novelty claim or evidence of integration between projects.

| Project | Documented role | Relationship to RelaySwarm |
|---|---|---|
| [P2P Media Loader](https://github.com/Novage/p2p-media-loader) | Peer-assisted media delivery; its [FAQ](https://github.com/Novage/p2p-media-loader/blob/main/FAQ.md#what-is-tracker) specifies WebTorrent-compatible trackers for WebRTC signalling | Closest HLS-engine comparison; RelaySwarm uses Nostr rendezvous and an experimental stream-author commitment contract |
| [Trystero](https://github.com/dmotz/trystero) | Generic WebRTC matchmaking and data/media APIs across several signalling strategies; the default package uses Nostr | Nostr-signalled browser transfer already exists; an HLS host still needs media-context, deadlines, provenance and consent integration |
| [MoQ working group](https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/moq/about/) | Media transport over QUIC with relay-capable distribution | A different transport/distribution design; RelaySwarm has no MoQ implementation |
| [Snowflake](https://snowflake.torproject.org/) | Volunteer proxies supporting access to Tor | A different application of volunteer connectivity; it does not establish HLS scheduling or RelaySwarm reachability |
| [RelaySwarmKit](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm-kit) | Swift Nostr rendezvous and encrypted SDP with a separate data-channel transport | Related implementation, but its README describes wire version 2 while the shared session here uses version 3; current interoperability is unverified |

P2P Media Loader's FAQ recommends operated tracker infrastructure for production;
multiple trackers can be selected. Nostr relays are also operated infrastructure
whose policy and capacity must be tested. Neither design removes the HTTP origin.

## The project's scope

RelaySwarm evaluates application-selected Nostr relays as the rendezvous path for
peer-assisted HLS. [NIP-53](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/53.md)
kind-30311 events can advertise relay information. The current host passes its
trusted stream event and network policy explicitly; automatic stream discovery
and policy extraction are not implemented.

The release adds a bounded hls.js loader, origin deadlines, admission callbacks,
upload opt-in, an origin-only mode and author-signed media commitments. Those
capabilities are documented in [INTEGRATION.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/INTEGRATION.md). They do not
establish an accepted NIP, broad ABR scheduling, production readiness or
compatibility with another implementation.

## Historical relay measurements

The August 2026 CLI/fan-out runs recorded acceptance of experimental kinds
24170/24171 on relay.damus.io, nos.lol and relay.primal.net and approximately
0.57 s average fan-out signalling. Recorded Chrome/Safari transfers finished
inside a common four-second segment. These are dated feasibility observations,
not relay service guarantees or mobile-loader validation; the original CLI
signalled plaintext SDP. [Spike results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/spikes/RESULTS.md) retain provenance.

Current release evidence includes desktop Chrome playback and a twelve-viewer
loopback soak. Separate-network performance and stronger adversarial tests
remain outstanding, as listed in [Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md).

---

Source: [docs/MAINTAINING-DOCS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/MAINTAINING-DOCS.md)

# Maintaining RelaySwarm documentation

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) · [Changelog](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/CHANGELOG.md)

## Public entry points

The current public documentation surface is the GitHub repository. There is no
configured standalone documentation site. README and `docs/README.md` provide
human navigation; package metadata and GitHub description/topics identify the
actual technologies and experimental status.

AI readers can use the
[raw index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/llms.txt)
or [full context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/llms-full.txt).
The index follows the [llms.txt proposal](https://llmstxt.org/): a title, summary,
scope notes and groups of annotated Markdown links. The optional full file is
generated from authored guides, with relative links resolved to public sources.
It excludes historical spike receipts/code; the index links that evidence separately.

These files make public information easier to retrieve. They do not prove that
search engines or assistants have crawled, indexed or recommended RelaySwarm,
and they do not grant crawler permission or change GitHub's robots policy.

## Edit and verify

1. Update authored Markdown, `llms.txt` and relevant package metadata from the
   implementation. Label dated evidence and planned work explicitly.
2. Run `npm run docs:generate` to rebuild `llms-full.txt`. Do not edit it by hand.
3. Run `npm run check:docs` and `npm run check`.
4. Commit authored and generated files together. CI runs the documentation check.
5. After merge, fetch the public raw files and compare them with the merged
   content. Check GitHub description/topics and release links separately.

`check:docs` requires only Node built-ins: it checks local/public-repository
Markdown link targets and local heading anchors, AI-index file-list structure,
documented module exports, command names and generated-context freshness. It
does not assert external website availability or rendering, and skips code
blocks when checking links. Verify external factual claims against primary sources
when updating them, rather than trusting an old comparison date.

## Release versus current documentation

The immutable v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 tags and downloadable assets contain release-time
documentation. Main-branch guides can correct examples and claims afterwards.
Use [Getting started](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md) for pinned installation and
[Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) for the release checkpoint. Never retag or silently replace
release assets to make a documentation correction.

Keep package, wire, commitment and metrics versions distinct. Preserve the
original CLI's plaintext-SDP and same-peer-digest limitations. Treat signed media
integrity, upload consent, phone acceptance, NAT reachability, hosted CI and public
distribution as separate claims. `peerFirstBytes` and upload quota counters are
not total network-data or financial-savings measurements.

## Future documentation hosting

If a public documentation site is added, publish its Markdown, an applicable
`llms.txt`, canonical URLs, navigation and search metadata as part of that site's
deployment. Verify its actual public responses before claiming discovery or
deployment. Do not add fictional domains, indexing guarantees or unsupported
production/security claims to this repository's metadata.

Source: [docs/BROADCASTING.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md)

# Broadcaster source workflow

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Operations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/OPERATIONS.md) · [Container deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md) · [Evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

This guide describes the 0.2.0 source broadcaster workflow, persistent publisher state and operator/reporting controls. Use the [current source candidate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/GETTING-STARTED.md); the immutable v0.1.0 assets do not include these additions. Publication of a guide does not establish deployed playback or platform acceptance.

## Local source and dependencies

Use Node 24 and ffmpeg with libx264 and AAC. RTMPS input/forwarding additionally requires a DNS hostname and FFmpeg major version 5 or later built with GnuTLS, or major version 8 or later built with OpenSSL. Install the source dependencies and the pinned MediaMTX router:

```sh
npm ci
npm run broadcast:install
```

The installer downloads MediaMTX 1.21.2 for macOS/Linux x64 or arm64, checks the archive against a platform-specific pinned SHA-256 before extraction, and prints the executable path. Its owner-controlled cache is `artifacts/tools/mediamtx-v1.21.2`; a private receipt records the extracted binary digest. A cached receipt is trusted local state, not independent upstream attestation. On another platform supply your own compatible router executable.

Start the bundled local router and broadcaster from the repository root:

```sh
npm run broadcast -- \
  --mediamtx artifacts/tools/mediamtx-v1.21.2/mediamtx \
  --state-dir artifacts/broadcast
```

Configure OBS Custom streaming with server `rtmp://127.0.0.1:1935/live` and an empty stream key. Supply **both H.264 video and AAC audio**. The bundled router listens only on loopback, refuses a second publisher for `live`, and exposes its RTSP read path at `rtsp://127.0.0.1:8554/live`. The launcher reads that path over TCP. Without `--mediamtx`, run the router separately or provide `--input` for an existing supported network source. Supported input schemes are RTSP, RTMP, RTMPS and SRT. RTSPS is rejected because verified TLS behaviour is not portable across supported FFmpeg versions; scheme acceptance does not prove compatibility with every source.

The launcher first binds a waiting listener and prints its address, normally `http://localhost:8787`. The root page returns HTTP 200 and checks again every three seconds. Before both HLS renditions publish, other endpoints return bounded HTTP 503 responses with `Retry-After: 3`; there is no session, relay or operator API on the waiting listener. Once output is ready, the launcher replaces that listener with the player on the same port. A waiting page proves HTTP availability, not media playback. Stop with Ctrl-C for orderly listener, worker and router shutdown.

An external OBS workstation can use an authorised SSH tunnel rather than a public plaintext RTMP listener:

```sh
ssh -N -L 1935:127.0.0.1:1935 deploy@your-host
```

OBS then targets its own loopback address. The container router uses an internal app/router network plus a separate normal bridge needed for its loopback RTMP port publication; RTSP has no published host port. Container ingest mappings and the existing/new HTTPS proxy choices are in the [deployment guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md). Remote browsers require configured TLS or an explicit `--public-url https://your-hostname` behind an HTTPS proxy. The public origin must match browser Origin headers. Configure repeated `--relay wss://...` options if using external relays; otherwise the server supplies its own bounded relay at `/relay`. `--stun` accepts a STUN URL; this launcher does not provide TURN credentials or a TURN deployment.

## Output and recovery

The encoder produces two fixed H.264/AAC renditions:

| Rendition | Frame shape/rate | Target video rate | Audio |
|---|---|---|---|
| low | 640 × 360, 30 fps | 700 kbps | AAC, 128 kbps, 48 kHz stereo |
| high | 1280 × 720, 30 fps | 2,500 kbps | AAC, 128 kbps, 48 kHz stereo |

Scaling preserves aspect ratio and pads to the fixed frame shape. Each rendition uses a two-second segment target and a twelve-segment live playlist: approximately **24 seconds of listed media**, not a 120-second playlist. ffmpeg retains an additional deletion tail; prior process generations have a separate two-minute pruning grace by default. These durations are storage/publication policy, not a measured end-to-end latency guarantee. Both renditions belong to one supported codec/frame-rate family; this is a fixed ladder, not a general encoding service.

The HLS worker and optional forwarding worker retry independently, with bounded exponential delay. Each HLS process generation uses a distinct segment directory and a persisted discontinuity sequence. Variant/master publication uses atomic file replacement. Source loss leaves the last published playlists available while workers reconnect; old HTTP availability does not establish fresh media or successful decoder recovery. Inspect publication age in operator status.

Use a dedicated canonical state directory owned by the launching user, preferably mode **0700**, with no symlink components or group/world writes. New directories use 0700. The launcher keeps `publisher.json` and `operator-token` as owner-only **0600**, regular, single-link files. The publisher file contains a private signing key and its signed redistribution authorisation; neither secret is delivered in browser sessions or operator status. Existing malformed/mismatched publisher state is rejected rather than replaced. Restarting with the same state retains publisher identity, swarm ID and authorisation; starting with another state directory creates another identity.

Only one pipeline may use a media directory. `/state/media/.broadcast-lock` in the container, or `STATE_DIR/media/.broadcast-lock` natively, is acquired exclusively. Orderly close removes it. An unclean exit may leave it and the next start fails closed. Stop all possible users of that volume/directory and establish exclusive ownership before manual stale-lock removal; never infer safety from a PID in a different namespace or delete locks automatically. See [operations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/OPERATIONS.md#restart-and-recovery).

## Optional RTMPS forwarding

Create a private, owner-controlled directory outside the checkout. In it, use a private editor to write one line containing the complete RTMPS ingest URL to a regular, single-link file owned by the launching user, mode **0600**. Keep the parent mode **0700** and use its canonical path. Start with:

```sh
npm run broadcast -- \
  --mediamtx artifacts/tools/mediamtx-v1.21.2/mediamtx \
  --state-dir artifacts/broadcast \
  --youtube-url-file /absolute/private/directory/youtube-url
```

The file supplies the URL without putting the stream key in environment variables or launcher arguments. For RTMPS input or forwarding, the pipeline first checks the selected executable’s version/build configuration with a five-second, 32 KiB output budget, before creating media state or workers. Direct callers of the argument builders must perform equivalent capability validation themselves. Forwarding has its own ffmpeg process and source reader, copies the H.264/AAC tracks into FLV, requires RTMPS, explicitly enables TLS certificate/hostname verification and sets a 15-second output I/O timeout. It does not transcode for a platform's separate compatibility rules. A forwarding outage cannot block the HLS process, although both still depend on the same source and host resources.

Trusted host/container administrators can inspect ffmpeg's process arguments, which contain the full ingest URL. The implementation consumes upstream stderr without publishing credentials in logs, metrics or browser sessions. Protect the host, secret file and process-inspection permissions accordingly. Restart the broadcaster to read a changed URL. A process marked running/connecting or repeated restarts is **not** evidence that YouTube accepted the stream or that viewers can play it; confirm that separately in an authorised platform test.

## Verification boundary

The release includes native process/publication tests and actual Chrome fixtures. A short HTTPS/WSS pilot with a synthetic source has a passing receipt; an earlier hosted MSE append failure remains unresolved. Physical-device, separate-network/NAT, sustained-operation, actual OBS and YouTube acceptance remain open. The dated [status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md) records both passing and failing evidence and its scope.

---

Source: [docs/NIP-DRAFT.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NIP-DRAFT.md)

# RelaySwarm experimental protocol draft

This is a local specification of the implemented RelaySwarm session and browser
object contracts. It is **not an accepted Nostr NIP**. Session wire version 3,
commitment schemas 1 and 2, the browser object framing and native object framing
have separate version boundaries. The original `poc.mjs` uses older plaintext
signalling and must not be described as this encrypted contract.

## Session events

Every event uses NIP-01 canonical serialisation and a valid BIP-340 signature.
The swarm identifier is exactly one `x` tag. Signal events have exactly one `p`
recipient tag. Presence events must not contain recipient tags. Senders use
throwaway Nostr identities; presence does not establish a trusted media author.

| Contract | Implemented value |
|----------|-------------------|
| Presence kind | `24170` |
| Signal kind | `24171` |
| Session version | JSON field `v: 3` |
| Signal encryption | Pairwise NIP-44 v2; mandatory |
| Sender event age | At most 120 seconds old; at most 30 seconds ahead |
| Presence JSON limit | 16 KiB UTF-8 |
| Signal ciphertext limit | 64 KiB UTF-8 |
| Decrypted signal limit | 8 KiB UTF-8 |
| Relay frame limit | 1 MiB |

Presence content has this shape:

```json
{"v":3,"role":"watcher","transports":[{"type":"webrtc","publicKey":"<64 lowercase hex characters>"}],"have":[],"open":true}
```

`role` and transport `type` are lowercase tokens, up to 32 characters, matching
`[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`. `transports` is required and contains at most eight entries.
`have` is required and contains at most 32 lowercase 64-character hexadecimal
object keys. `open` is optional and advisory. An optional opaque `ticket` is a
non-empty string of at most 2 KiB UTF-8; admission is the host's responsibility.
A browser WebRTC capability uses the peer's Nostr public key. A native
`hyperdht-v1` capability uses its DHT transport public key.

Signal plaintext has this shape, then the whole JSON object is NIP-44 encrypted:

```json
{"v":3,"type":"offer","transport":"webrtc","requestId":"<request identifier>","payload":{"sdp":"<complete SDP>"}}
```

`type` and `transport` use the same token rule. `requestId` is 8–64 ASCII
characters from `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]`. `payload` is an object. Browser offers, answers
and rejects must match the pending counterparty, transport and request ID.
SDP appears in `payload.sdp`. Browser admission is checked before revealing an
answer and again after asynchronous negotiation. Native `dial` and `ready`
payloads bind the transport public key, expected SHA-256 and exact object size;
see [Native transport](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/NATIVE-TRANSPORT.md).

A peer must not reinterpret a missing version or an unsupported version as
plaintext. RelaySwarm's current session rejects version 2. The NIP-44 encryption
version is not the RelaySwarm session version.

## Browser object exchange

A WebRTC data channel carries JSON text controls and binary chunks. At most one
response is in flight in each direction. A binary chunk is at most 16 KiB.

| Message | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `{"t":"have","keys":["<key>"]}` | Complete advertised key set, capped at 256 |
| `{"t":"have","add":["<key>"],"del":[]}` | Bounded key-set update |
| `{"t":"want","id":1,"k":"<key>"}` | Request one object |
| `{"t":"meta","id":1,"size":262181}` | Exact response size; chunks follow |
| Binary messages | Response bytes, serialised between `meta` and `eof` |
| `{"t":"eof","id":1}` | Response complete |
| `{"t":"none","id":1}` | Object unavailable or serving declined |

Control text is capped at 64 KiB. Object size is limited by the host's configured
segment cap, at most 16 MiB. `meta` cannot override the independently verified
commitment size. Repeated headers, excessive chunks, empty chunks and response
size overflow fail the transfer. Timeout or cancellation closes a receiving
link, because untagged late binary chunks cannot safely be reused by another
request. Upload queues and backpressure have bounded capacities and deadlines.
Optional `contribution` and `fetching` controls coordinate serving and short
fetch leases; they are advisory and never authorise media or spend upload
allowance.

An object key identifies the host's canonical media URL/range within a swarm;
it is **not** the content digest. The local publisher uses SHA-256 over
`swarmId + "\n" + path`, appending `#start-end` for an exclusive-end byte range.
Hosts with CDN aliases or query-bearing URLs must define their trust policy
explicitly. A peer's `have` claim or `meta` message never establishes provenance.

## Signed media commitments

Commitments use kind `24172`, one `x` swarm tag and one `e` tag naming the stable
stream authorisation event. That event is signed by the trusted media author,
has kind `30311`, one `d` identifier and explicit
`["relayswarm","redistribute","1"]` consent.

Schema 1 uses domain `relayswarm-segment-v1` and binds the stream event ID, swarm,
object key, numeric rendition, sequence, discontinuity, part index or `null`,
SHA-256, exact size and expiry. Schema 2 uses `relayswarm-segment-v2` and adds
`playlist`, `mediaType` and `encryption`; its `rendition` is the exact playlist
identity. This avoids treating player level indices, which codec filtering can
renumber, as trusted media identities. Content must equal the canonical field
order emitted by `commitmentContent` in
[segment-commitment.mjs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/src/browser/segment-commitment.mjs).

The receiver independently matches every context field. Commitments are at
most 120 seconds old, at most 30 seconds ahead and expire within 300 seconds of
verification. The local publisher normally signs for 60 seconds. Size is
positive and within the host's segment cap. The actual received bytes must
match the signed size and SHA-256 before delivery to the player.

Schema 2 permits alternate audio and complete LL-HLS parts. Delta playlists
require a bounded previously verified catalogue; a cold delta cannot establish
omitted contexts. Init maps remain HTTP assets. Identity AES-128 requires an
explicit publication policy and signs ciphertext plus exact key URI/IV
metadata. Content keys stay on the HTTP path and are never peer objects.
SAMPLE-AES, DRM, subtitle and I-frame rendition publication are unsupported.

## Scoped commitment delegation

Kind `24173`, domain `relayswarm-commitment-delegation-v1`, authorises one
commitment public key under the trusted author's signature. Its canonical
content binds `streamEventId`, `swarmId`, `delegatePubkey`, `notBefore`,
`expiresAt`, `renditions`, `mediaTypes`, `allowParts` and `maxSegmentBytes`.
Scopes contain at most 40 exact rendition identifiers. Delegation expires no
later than one hour after issuance. A delegated commitment includes
`["delegation","<delegation event ID>"]`, matches every scope restriction and
cannot outlive the delegation.

Kind `24174`, domain `relayswarm-commitment-revocation-v1`, revokes an exact
delegation ID under the same author's signature, stream and swarm. Hosts supply
a bounded current revocation view or explicit revoked IDs. Verifiers do not
query relays and absence from a supplied view does not prove global absence of
revocation. Replacing the trusted stream authorisation also invalidates scopes
bound to its old event ID. A delegate is not authorised to sign live metadata.

## Live metadata and stable authorisation

The local publisher keeps the minimal commitment authorisation stable across
restarts. A separate full NIP-53 kind `30311` advertisement uses address
`live-<stable authorisation event ID>`, so renewing live status does not replace
the event to which commitments and delegations bind. Its signed tags include
`streaming`, `status`, `starts`, `expiration`, `relays`,
`relayswarm-authorisation` and `relayswarm-swarm`. Ended advertisements include
`ends`. The RelaySwarm-specific linking tags are experimental extensions.

Advertisements expire within five minutes and require HTTPS/WSS endpoints.
Loopback HTTP/WS requires explicit test opt-in. Discovery pins the linked
stable authorisation using `streamAuthorisations`, checks the same author and
host-selected swarm, and preserves the host's allowed origins, relay and ICE
policies. Event-suggested endpoints cannot expand those policies. The latest
ended, withdrawn or unsafe update suppresses older live metadata. The host
must obtain current metadata; a stable signature alone does not prove that a
stream is still live. `previousEvent` gives immediate lifecycle updates a later
creation timestamp within the allowed clock tolerance, avoiding an addressable
event ID tie. Standard NIP-53 fields are described in the
[upstream draft](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/53.md).

## Historical Swift baseline and current interoperability

On 13 October 2026, `test/interop-swift.mjs` tested public RelaySwarmKit revision
[`7eb042ee0fc0e960780c61d755a2ec50f1a8be40`](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm-kit/tree/7eb042ee0fc0e960780c61d755a2ec50f1a8be40)
with its pinned secp256k1 dependency and macOS arm64 libdatachannel binary.

| Gate | Measured result |
|------|-----------------|
| Unmodified Kit `SwarmSignaller` ↔ RelaySwarm v3 | Incompatible in both directions |
| Kit NIP-44/signatures ↔ JavaScript | Compatible in the exercised encrypted session |
| Explicit Swift v3 fixture adapter ↔ JavaScript session | Encrypted presence/offer/answer journey passed |
| Kit libdatachannel ↔ JavaScript werift/production `PeerLink` | 262,181-byte transfer in 17 chunks passed |
| Independent Swift commitment verification | 12 schema/context/signature/expiry cases passed |
| Corrupted bytes over the real WebRTC channel | Rejected against the signed commitment |
| Plaintext and malformed encrypted session probes | Rejected by the fixture adapter |
| Published Swift v3 client, physical devices, NAT variety | Not proved at that baseline checkpoint |
| Kit ↔ HyperDHT native transport | Unsupported by the inspected Kit |

The test adapter uses unchanged pinned toolkit crypto, relay and WebRTC
components, but adds a separate strict v3 envelope parser and browser object
receiver inside this repository. Its passing journey **does not establish
compatibility of the Kit client at that revision**. That baseline Kit uses
presence version 2, signal version tags and top-level `type`/`sdp`, and retains a
plaintext fallback. Current RelaySwarm accepts none of those as v3 sessions.

Run `node test/interop-swift.mjs --evidence artifacts/relayswarm-swift-interop-current.json`
on macOS arm64 with Swift and authenticated read-only `gh` access. It fetches
exact public component sources into an owned scratch package, compiles with four
jobs, records source hashes and results, then removes its downloads/build and
fixture services after success. The named receipt is retained. A failed build
keeps owned scratch for diagnosis and reuse; remove it once its evidence is
recorded. No external repository is edited.

### Historical Kit migration requirements

These requirements guided the subsequent RelaySwarmKit upgrade:

1. Update `Sources/RelaySwarmSignalling/Swarm.swift` to emit/require `v:3`,
   transport, request ID and nested payloads; require NIP-44 for every signal.
   Remove automatic plaintext fallback from the default API. If legacy support
   remains, expose it through a separately named opt-in API and never negotiate
   down from v3.
2. Extend presence with bounded transport capabilities, object keys, optional
   upload availability and opaque host admission tickets. Apply the v3 age,
   recipient uniqueness, payload and byte limits before dispatch.
3. Update `Sources/RelaySwarmTransport/SwarmHost.swift` so answers preserve the
   pending request ID and transport, with admission before disclosing SDP.
   Supply bounded `have`/`want`/`meta`/binary/`eof` framing rather than assuming
   arbitrary host broadcasts are authenticated HLS objects.
4. Add an independent signed commitment module covering schemas 1 and 2,
   current author/delegation/revocation trust, exact fragment context and byte
   verification. Preserve receive-only/upload-consent semantics in the consuming
   application; a verified commitment is not viewer consent to serve.
5. Run this real interop journey against the updated public APIs, without the
   fixture adapter, and add Swift negative tests for version downgrade,
   misrouted/replayed events, context confusion, chunk floods and cancellation.
   Release and pin that tested Kit revision before publishing compatibility
   claims. HyperDHT support would be a separate transport implementation.


The concrete [Kit review proposal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/interop/README.md) includes an exact-source
patch and SHA-256 manifest. Its full local SDK suite passed 25 tests with one
public-relay test skipped. The later authorised upgrade adds public signed-media
APIs and is published as [Kit v0.5.0](https://github.com/forgesworn/relayswarm-kit/releases/tag/v0.5.0)
at `2f0b26ace4096a5dca87baf715274f91c331ac3a`. PR and merged-head CI passed
39 tests with one opt-in public-relay skip. The production browser sender and
current `SwarmGuest`, `MediaDataChannel` and `SignedMediaTransfer` APIs completed
author/delegate transfers of 108,950 fMP4 HLS bytes; corruption, tampering and
pre-request/during-transfer revocation each returned zero bytes. No wire adapter
was used. The exact source/receipt boundary and remaining physical/NAT/playback
responsibilities are in the [interop guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/interop/README.md).

---

Source: [docs/OPERATIONS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/OPERATIONS.md)

# Pilot operator controls

[Documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/README.md) · [Broadcaster](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/BROADCASTING.md) · [Container deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md) · [API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md) · [Evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md)

These controls belong to the **0.2.0 source candidate** and are absent from v0.1.0 assets. The candidate adds bounded admission, durable reporting and crash supervision; final production acceptance remains open. See [production features](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/PRODUCTION-FEATURES.md) and [Status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/STATUS.md).

Before the first broadcast is ready, the root returns an HTTP 200 waiting page with a three-second refresh. Other endpoints return HTTP 503 with `Retry-After: 3`, including the authenticated status route; the waiting listener exposes no session, relay or operator API. The launcher replaces it with the player on the same port when both renditions publish. Waiting-page reachability does not establish fresh media, successful decoding or a verified public deployment.

## Credentials and HTTP routes

The broadcaster creates its private `operator-token` in `--state-dir`. The demo can instead take `--operator-token-file FILE`, the `RELAYSWARM_OPERATOR_TOKEN` environment variable, or the `startDemoServer` JavaScript option `operatorToken`. Prefer a private file; supplying both JavaScript token sources is rejected. Tokens must contain 32–256 non-whitespace characters. Token files require an owner-controlled canonical parent, a 0600 regular single-link file and matching ownership; symlinks and unsafe permissions are rejected.

The token is never in the player page, `/session.json`, public policy or operator status. Keep it separate from publisher signing secrets and forwarding credentials. The [deployment guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md#operator-access-and-private-identity) shows private header-file extraction and curl commands without printing the token or placing it in arguments.

| Route | Method/authentication | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `/operator/status` | GET, `Authorization: Bearer TOKEN` | Policy, origin HTTP counters, publisher work/cache metrics, report aggregate and optional redacted broadcast worker/publication status |
| `/operator/policy` | POST, bearer token, `application/json` | Accepts only `{"mode":null}`, `{"mode":"off"}`, `{"mode":"shadow"}` or `{"mode":"peer-first"}`; returns incremented policy revision |
| `/delivery-policy.json` | GET, public | Mode, revision and reporting availability; no token or publisher secret |
| `/reports` | POST, explicit server enablement and same-origin browser request | Accepts only bounded numeric measurement fields |
| `/operator/admission` | POST, bearer token | Revokes a key or rotates the ticket epoch |
| `/admission/challenge`, `/admission/ticket`, `/admission/verify` | POST, same-origin | Bounded key-possession challenge, short-lived ticket and live verification |

Unconfigured operator controls return 503; absent/incorrect credentials return 401. Cross-site Origin/Fetch-Metadata requests are rejected. Operator bodies are capped at 2,048 bytes and reject unknown fields/invalid modes; wrong methods and content types are rejected. Authentication is not a replacement for HTTPS, host protection or restricting administrative exposure at the reverse proxy. The bearer token grants policy/status access, not media-source credentials or shell access.

## Policy and viewer consent

`mode: null` leaves mode choice to the viewer. `off` requests origin-only playback. `shadow` or `peer-first` selects behaviour **only after the viewer has chosen a peer mode**: viewer origin-only selection and `Use origin only` always win. A policy can never opt the viewer into uploading. Valid publisher-signed redistribution authorisation is also required by the browser engine; operator policy is not an authorisation bypass.

The page polls policy and the publisher session every two seconds, with a single in-flight poll and five-second fetch budgets. Disablement is cooperative browser behaviour, not an immediate revocation of already delivered media or a claim that every client honours policy. On operator off or policy/session failure, it restores origin loading and clears the upload checkbox. Later enablement leaves uploading off until the viewer opts in again. Playback's video instance remains running; origin availability still determines whether playback can continue. Session identity changes on the same manifest trigger swarm rejoining without resetting page counters or reloading the playback instance. A changed manifest requires an appropriate host-page transition; this page fails to origin rather than guessing.

## Upload and measurement limits

The page offers 10 MB, 100 MB (default) or 1 GB of cumulative **media payload** allowance, plus a separate upload rate choice. Web Locks and origin storage reserve payloads atomically across settings, rejoining, reloads and tabs. Interrupted sends are not refunded; oversized next segments do not spend the smaller balance. Exhaustion stops contribution while playback continues. Storage failure disables uploading. Consent is requested anew after reload; the viewer can explicitly raise or reset the allowance. It is not an account-wide or physical wire-traffic cap.

The library option is `maxUploadBytesPerSession`; omission means unlimited and zero means no media uploads. Its metrics expose configured cap, remaining allowance and exhaustion. Host applications that recreate a swarm must carry their own cumulative allowance forward, as the page does. Rate limits use a token bucket with up to a two-second burst. Signalling, transport overhead, commitment fetches and shadow downloads are additional traffic; an upload media cap is not a wire-traffic limit.

Server `origin` counters separate `/media/` requests/body bytes from commitment requests/body bytes. Media counts include playlists, init segments, ranges and error responses; HEAD contributes no response body. Body bytes are bytes handed to HTTP responses, not confirmed physical-wire totals or network overhead. Browser resource timings have their own scope and exclude native-HLS requests. Verified peer payload records media accepted from peers; shadow mode adds peer traffic alongside origin loading. None of these counters alone establish net traffic/cost savings.

Publisher metrics include signing/hashing/cache activity, concurrent work and rejections. Broadcast metrics include worker states/restarts, rendition shape, generation and last publication time; they contain no input/output URLs or stream keys. A running process does not prove a fresh source, successful decoding or platform acceptance.

## Optional numeric reporting

Reporting is **off by default**. Enable it server-side using `--telemetry` or `startDemoServer({telemetry:true})`; each viewer must then check the separate reporting opt-in. The page sends cumulative numeric snapshots every fifteen seconds after playback starts. Downloadable field receipts remain separate and are not submitted.

Reports use `{v:1, reportId, sequence, values}`. The temporary page ID is 32 hex characters; sequence increases for new cumulative snapshots. Values contain exactly `durationMs`, `peerBytes`, `uploadedBytes`, `originMediaRequests`, `originMediaBytes`, `stalls`, `stallMs` and `fatalErrors`, non-negative safe integers up to 10¹². No account, browser version, device/network labels or peer IP addresses are accepted. Infrastructure still sees connection addresses; there is no third-party report endpoint.

The collector permits 240 requests per ten seconds, caps bodies at 2,048 bytes and requires same-origin requests. Retention defaults to 256 page IDs for five minutes; `reportCapacity` and `reportTtlMs` bound it. With `operatorState` (CLI `--operator-state`) enabled, private state survives restart and expiry is applied after reopening. Retries are idempotent, stale sequences do not add traffic again, and decreased counters are refused. The pending durable write queue defaults to 64; overload returns 503. Reports remain untrusted observations, not unique-viewer totals or billing evidence. Broadcasters enable private operational persistence automatically.

## Resources and admission boundary

The HTTP example caps active media responses at 32, connections at 128, header size at 8 KiB and request/header timeouts at ten seconds. Commitment requests have a separate 240-per-ten-second budget. Publisher defaults permit eight concurrent commitment operations and 512 entries in each hash/commitment cache; playlist/catalogue/segment bounds are documented in the [API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/docs/API.md). Cancellation releases media file handles and response slots even while lookup/opening is pending.

The [container package](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md) sets CPU, memory, process and log limits, loopback ingest/player mappings and private network boundaries. Its healthcheck requires a recent publication and publishing worker state; it becomes unhealthy without input or during a prolonged source outage. Compose restart policies recover container exits, not unhealthy status alone. Measure actual host capacity before broadening a pilot.

The candidate demo supplies a bounded ticket issuer and live revocation checks. The embedded relay rejects unadmitted presence/signals and caps aggregate messages. Open issuance establishes bounded keys, not unique people or paid subscriptions; broader Sybil and real-network acceptance remain separate gates.

## Restart and recovery

Preserve the dedicated state directory/volume to retain publisher identity and operator credentials. Shut down normally so workers, file handles and the exclusive `.broadcast-lock` are released. Do not run two pipelines against one media directory, mount the state into unrelated services, or delete private state during an upgrade.

On supported local POSIX storage, permanent publication/worker lease inodes and a guardian permit automatic parent-crash recovery after all worker groups are reaped. A dirty guardian marker or legacy pre-lease lock requires explicit operator inspection. Never delete lease database files to force acquisition. A namespace-local PID is insufficient evidence; retain private backups and leave uncertain ownership closed. The [deployment guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgesworn/relayswarm/main/deploy/README.md#exclusive-volume-ownership-and-crash-recovery) describes the recovery boundary.

Publisher state contains the signing secret; a whole-volume backup can also contain generated media. Use access-controlled encrypted backups. Forwarding credentials live in a separate private file and are read at launch; trusted process administrators can inspect ffmpeg's full URL arguments. Never put these secrets in a browser receipt, repository, public status response or issue attachment.
